question: I need to know a good quick summary of the Microsoft document or the research whatever it said about how the more context and continuity you give to an agent the better it's gonna help the human, I'm trying to make this case in a meeting next week and I need to be able to pull easily from the relevant statistics or research and whatever Microsoft has got that's like visually interesting and helpful for this
answer:
Short summary (one line)
- Microsoft’s 2025 New Future of Work report argues that giving AI agents continuity and shared context (recaps, handoffs, project history, “Ditto” context) shifts collaboration from one-shot outputs to ongoing augmentation — which improves usefulness but also creates new trust and verification needs.

Key evidence / citations you can quote in the meeting
- Trust vs verification (survey): Benzing et al., 2025 — survey of 1,800 global full‑time English‑speaking employees: about 2 in 3 employees report trusting AI agents, while ~60% skip accuracy checks on agent outputs. (New-Future-Of-Work-Report-2025.pdf — page 55, “Thinking, Learning, and Psychological Influences” section.)  
  - Why this matters: high baseline trust + low verification makes continuity features (recaps, handoffs, provenance) important so teams can catch mistakes and maintain accountability.
- Design/feature recommendations (qualitative, cited Microsoft work and field studies): the report synthesizes multiple Microsoft studies and related work that show benefits from adding temporal continuity features such as:
  - Instant recaps (summaries of past meetings/work) and Adaptive Handoff (giving the next person the relevant context), and Project Browsers (persistent project context). (New-Future-Of-Work-Report-2025.pdf — page 42, figure and nearby text in “AI for Teamwork”.)  
  - “Dittos” (mimetic agents) model a Source → Ditto Context → Recap cycle, explicitly using prepared context and recaps to extend availability while keeping collaborators apprised. (New-Future-Of-Work-Report-2025.pdf — page 49, “AI for Teamwork”.)
- Readiness / people factors: the report emphasizes team readiness (understanding which tasks suit humans vs agents, trust in agents, aligning on outcomes, skills to engage, openness to integration) as a cycle that supports safe adoption of agentic systems. (New-Future-Of-Work-Report-2025.pdf — page 55, “Team Agent Readiness” figure and nearby text.)

Two visuals from the report that illustrate the point
- Why include them: each is a compact visual you can drop into a slide to show (1) the specific features that provide continuity and (2) the human/team conditions needed for safe augmentation.

1) Timeline UI concept showing continuity features (Instant Recaps, Adaptive Handoff, Project Browsers) — illustrates concrete product patterns that add continuity across time.
![Source figure](fli-image:report-document:1:235)
Source: New-Future-Of-Work-Report-2025.pdf — page 42 (figure and nearby text in “AI for Teamwork”).
- What this shows: concrete interface locations where context/continuity can be delivered (retrospection → prospection → handoff → future planning). Good to illustrate “how” to give continuity.
- What it does NOT establish: no quantitative effect sizes in the figure — it’s a design concept, not an outcome measurement.

2) Team Agent Readiness cycle — shows the human/team capabilities that make contextual/continuous agents effective.
![Source figure](fli-image:report-document:1:244)
Source: New-Future-Of-Work-Report-2025.pdf — page 55 (“Workplace learning and experimentation create a cycle for Agentic AI adoption”; adjacent text notes Benzing et al., 2025 results).
- What this shows: to get the gains from context and continuity you need team alignment, trust, skills, and willingness to integrate agents.
- What it does NOT establish: again, qualitative — it doesn’t show measured productivity gains for a specific continuity feature.

Quick, meeting-ready talking points (30–60 seconds)
- “Microsoft’s synthesis says the next leverage from AI isn’t single answers but continuity: agents that carry context (recaps, handoffs, project history, Dittos) let humans build on earlier work rather than re-start each time.” (cite: Microsoft NFW Report 2025, “AI for Teamwork”, pp. 42, 49)
- “But there’s a catch: a global survey (n=1,800) found ~2/3 of employees already trust agents, yet ~60% skip checking outputs — so continuity must come with explainability and recap/provenance so teams don’t silently accept errors.” (cite: Microsoft NFW Report 2025, p. 55, Benzing et al., 2025)
- “Design implication: invest in persistent context (recaps + adaptive handoff + project browsers) and team readiness (alignment on outcomes, training) to convert agent continuity into real productivity and reduce risk.” (cite: pp. 42, 49, 55)

Suggested slide headline + 3 bullets (copy‑paste)
- Headline: “Context + Continuity: Where AI actually augments work”
  - Bullet 1: “Agents that keep project context (recaps, handoffs, persistent project views) let humans pick up work faster and build on prior decisions.” (Microsoft NFW Report 2025, p. 42)
  - Bullet 2: “Teams must be ready: trust + alignment + skill to engage with agents increases value and reduces surprises.” (Microsoft NFW Report 2025, p. 55)
  - Bullet 3 (evidence): “Survey (n=1,800): ~2/3 trust agents but ~60% skip accuracy checks — hence continuity needs explainability/recaps.” (Microsoft NFW Report 2025, p. 55)

Limitations and scope you should call out briefly in the meeting
- The figures in the report are mostly conceptual/design guidance (qualitative). They illustrate what to build, not exact measured productivity gains from a single feature.  
- The strongest numeric evidence in the report extract is the Benzing survey (trust + low verification); other cited studies are summarized or field studies referenced but the report text here does not always provide effect sizes in the figure captions. If you need precise measured improvements (e.g., X% faster handoffs), we’ll need to pull the original underlying studies (some are Microsoft field trials cited in the report).

If you want next
- I can extract the exact short quote(s) and page numbers to paste verbatim into your slide notes (e.g., the Benzing stat with the precise phrasing), or produce a single, slide-ready two-panel image (timeline + readiness cycle) arranged with source captions for your deck. Which would you prefer?

- Retrieved the actual figures referenced in the draft and expanded the source regions around them (selected pages from the Microsoft New Future of Work Report 2025) so claims are supported by the report text.

- Kept the selection tight — only the genuinely relevant figures for the “context + continuity helps agents augment humans” argument are included below. I did not invent or pad evidence.

Relevant figures (inline) — you can reuse these for an internal meeting
1) Concentric diagram: augmentation vs automation (qualitative framing)
![Source figure](fli-image:report-document:1:223)

- What it helps show: high-level framing that augmentation and new human+machine tasks are a much larger design opportunity than straightforward automation.
- What it does NOT establish: no numeric values or causal impact estimates — the figure is explicitly qualitative and conceptual (report text repeats that it’s an illustrative schematic).

2) Timeline UI concept (Instant Recaps, Adaptive Handoff, Project Browser)
![Source figure](fli-image:report-document:1:235)

- Source: New-Future-Of-Work-Report-2025.pdf — page 42, section “AI for Teamwork.”
- Text nearby (explicit, report text): “Three example design concepts from Vanukuru et al. (2025) demonstrating how AI interfaces can support ‘temporal work’ across collaborative workflows: (a) Instant Recaps … (b) Adaptive Meeting Handoff … (c) Project Browser …”
- What it helps show: concrete interface patterns where continuity (recaps, handoffs, persistent project context) would be delivered — useful to argue “this is how you give continuity.”
- What it does NOT establish: it’s a design concept, not a measured result; no effect sizes or experiment outcomes are shown on the figure itself.

3) Team Agent Readiness cycle (trust, skills, alignment, learning)
![Source figure](fli-image:report-document:1:244)

- Source: New-Future-Of-Work-Report-2025.pdf — page 55, section “Thinking, Learning, and Psychological Influences.” Caption (adjacent): “Workplace learning and experimentation create a cycle for Agentic AI adoption (Adapted from Benzing et al., 2025).”
- Key, quotable statistic from the report text (page 55): “Benzing et al.'s (2025) survey of 1,800 global full-time English‑speaking employees found that 2 in 3 employees report trusting AI agents; however, 60% skip accuracy checks in AI output.”
  - Exact sample description given in the report: n = 1,800 global full‑time, English‑speaking employees (Benzing et al., 2025).
- What it helps show: the human/team factors required to convert continuity into reliable augmentation — and an attitudinal risk (high trust + low verification) that makes recaps/provenance/visibility necessary.
- What it does NOT establish: the survey is attitudinal (trust/verification) and does not itself prove that adding continuity features causes X% productivity gains. It supports the design argument that continuity must be paired with oversight and training.

- Most figures in the report are conceptual/design visuals — they make the qualitative argument that continuity/context matters, and they show where to put features, but they do not provide measured causal effect sizes. · Automation-first approaches mainly remove cost from existing tasks, limiting gains to labor arbitrage and replication (Brynjolfsson, 2022; Autor, 2022).

· Strategies focused on augmentation and innovation can create new categories of work and value, driving positive- sum growth. For instance, Amazon's success came from reinventing retail through human-machine complementarity, not automating cashiers.

sections.text:
AI can drive goal clarity for effective meetings and smarter workflows

· As the clear expression of goals becomes increasingly vital in an Al world (Passi, 2025), meetings stand out as a key opportunity where improved goal articulation and communication can drive effective human collaboration (Scott et al., 2024).

· In a large-scale field study, Tankelevitch et al. (2025) find that workplace reflection on meeting goals can drive effective meeting behaviors across workflows, with many opportunities for AI assistance throughout the meeting life-cycle.

· Through brief reflective dialogue, Al improves meeting preparation by helping people clarify and express goals, transform them into actionable outputs, and take proactive collaborative actions to drive meeting effectiveness (Scott et al., 2025; Doherty et al., in prep.).

· Al interfaces can support tracking goals during meetings (Chen et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025b), as well as ensure the flow of goals between meetings and across workflows by supporting workers in prospective and retrospective thinking about goals (Vanukuru et al., 2025).

· When goals are externalized in this way, they become structured inputs for other forms of Al-driven collaboration, such as document creation or spec-driven development (GitHub, 2025).

Three example design concepts from Vanukuru et al. (2025) demonstrating how AI interfaces can support 'temporal work' across collaborative workflows: (a) Instant Recaps use AI to dynamically adapt their support for goal reflection based on the time people have after meetings, (b) Adaptive Meeting Handoff uses AI to support effective goal-driven transitions between disparate meetings, and (c) Project Browser allows people to explore and make sense of projects at different timescales.

Dittos: How mimetic AI agents can augment relationships

· Dittos are embodied, mimetic, reciprocal agents that look, sound, and discuss like the person who created them (Leong et al., 2024).

· The person represented by the Ditto (the Source), prepares the Context on topics that the Ditto can talk about on behalf of the Source, and gets apprised of any interactions with their Ditto through a Recap. The Source and Collaborators can build on any Ditto conversations in developing their ongoing relationship, extending their availability.

· While Dittos were originally developed for workplace settings, they are being explored in other settings as well:

· FamilyDittos: Connecting with remote family members, especially separated by inconvenient time zones. (Tanprasert et al., 2025).

· IRL Dittos: Connecting with remote colleagues by encountering their Dittos in shared, public spaces (like a hallway) (Lee et al., 2025).

· There are many questions about the responsible design of Dittos. Because a Ditto seems like someone people know, people believe Dittos more than GenAl. Researchers conducted Black Mirror Writers' Room exercises with the project team to proactively identify responsible design implications (Lee et al., 2023; Klassen & Fiesler, 2022).

sections.heading: Workplace learning can combat AI overreliance and cognitive atrophy
sections.text:
Workplace learning can combat AI overreliance and cognitive atrophy

· Blind trust (Benzing et al., 2025), overreliance (Passi et al., 2024), and cognitive offloading (Gerlich, 2025) are risks of human-Al interactions. Benzing et al.'s (2025) survey of 1,800 global full-time English-speaking employees found that 2 in 3 employees report trusting AI agents; however, 60% skip accuracy checks in AI output.

· Workplace learning plays a crucial role in combatting these risks, while also driving the employee engagement and resilience required for successful AI workforce transformation (Malik & Garg, 2017). Teams with strong Al readiness (including skills and literacy) report greater individual and collective value from Al, such as higher productivity, better decision- making, and more creative, collaborative teams (Benzing et al., 2025; Xue & Song, 2025).

· Human-Al interactions that are discursive and progressive promote cognitive enrichment and combat cognitive atrophy (Danry et al., 2023), which are the core elements of traditional Socratic learning methods used to develop metacognition and critical thinking.

· Given its ability to provide personalized, adaptive, role- and task-based learning while incorporating context, memory, and conversational turns, AI presents a promising new learning modality (Joshi, 2025; Tomitsu, 2025). There is opportunity to develop novel interactive learning experiences, like assessment-based dialogic questioning (Hung et al., 2024), to drive employee engagement through workplace upskilling.

Workplace learning and experimentation create a cycle for Agentic AI adoption (Adapted from Benzing et al., 2025).

· When goals are externalized in this way, they become structured inputs for other forms of Al-driven collaboration, such as document creation or spec-driven development (GitHub, 2025).

· Blind trust (Benzing et al., 2025), overreliance (Passi et al., 2024), and cognitive offloading (Gerlich, 2025) are risks of human-Al interactions. Benzing et al.'s (2025) survey of 1,800 global full-time English-speaking employees found that 2 in 3 employees report trusting AI agents; however, 60% skip accuracy checks in AI output.

· Workplace learning plays a crucial role in combatting these risks, while also driving the employee engagement and resilience required for successful AI workforce transformation (Malik & Garg, 2017). Teams with strong Al readiness (including skills and literacy) report greater individual and collective value from Al, such as higher productivity, better decision- making, and more creative, collaborative teams (Benzing et al., 2025; Xue & Song, 2025).

· Human-Al interactions that are discursive and progressive promote cognitive enrichment and combat cognitive atrophy (Danry et al., 2023), which are the core elements of traditional Socratic learning methods used to develop metacognition and critical thinking.

· Given its ability to provide personalized, adaptive, role- and task-based learning while incorporating context, memory, and conversational turns, AI presents a promising new learning modality (Joshi, 2025; Tomitsu, 2025). There is opportunity to develop novel interactive learning experiences, like assessment-based dialogic questioning (Hung et al., 2024), to drive employee engagement through workplace upskilling.
